claim: Dopamine plays an important role in hippocampal long-term memory.
source: An important role of dopamine in hippocampal long-term memory has long been recognised (O'Carroll et al., 2006; Rossato et al., 2009; Shohamy and Adcock, 2010; Takeuchi et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Long-term memory is thought to be encoded by synaptic plasticity, in particular long-term potentiation (LTP).
source: Long-term memory is thought to be encoded by synaptic plasticity, in particular long-term potentiation (LTP; Bliss and Lomo, 1973)
evidence: Supported by citation to foundational work and established scientific understanding

claim: LTP has been divided into an early phase and a protein-synthesis-dependent late phase based on its duration.
source: which, based on its duration, has been divided into an early phase and a protein-synthesis-dependent late phase (Frey et al., 1988).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Dopaminergic signalling has been implicated specifically in 'late-phase' LTP (L-LTP).
source: Dopaminergic signalling has been implicated specifically in 'late-phase' LTP (L-LTP; Frey et al., 1990; Huang and Kandel, 1995; Matthies et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Dopamine acts on G-protein-coupled receptors which activate adenylate cyclases (AC) to generate cAMP.
source: Dopamine acts on G-protein-coupled receptors which activate adenylate cyclases (AC) to generate cAMP, which in turn activates several effectors, including the cAMP-dependent protein kinase (PKA).
evidence: Draws from established understanding of dopamine receptor signaling

claim: cAMP activates several effectors, including the cAMP-dependent protein kinase (PKA).
source: Dopamine acts on G-protein-coupled receptors which activate adenylate cyclases (AC) to generate cAMP, which in turn activates several effectors, including the cAMP-dependent protein kinase (PKA).
evidence: Draws from established understanding of cAMP signaling

claim: PKA has several downstream targets which ultimately regulate transcription and translation.
source: PKA has several downstream targets which ultimately regulate transcription and translation (Sassone-Corsi, 1995; Kebabian and Calne, 1979; Mayr and Montminy, 2001; Smith et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Dopamine increases protein synthesis in hippocampal neurons.
source: We found that dopamine increases protein synthesis in hippocampal neurons.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from puromycin labeling assays shown in Figure 1

claim: Slices incubated with PMY showed a significantly higher PMY intensity than those without.
source: As expected, slices incubated with PMY showed a significantly higher PMY intensity than those without (control, 0.39±0.02 a.u., n=9, vs +PMY, 0.54±0.03, t(16) = 4.0, p=0.001, n=9; Figure 1B and C)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental measurements shown in Figure 1B and C

claim: 30 min preincubation with 10 µM CHX significantly reduced the PMY signal.
source: We found that 30 min preincubation with 10 µM CHX significantly reduced the PMY signal, confirming the specificity of the labelling approach (PMY, 1.8±0.45, n=7 vs PMY + CHX, 0.4±0.05, n=8, t(6) = 3.1, p=0.02; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B

claim: 2 hr preincubation with 0.5 mM AM significantly reduced the PMY signal.
source: as did 2 hr preincubation with 0.5 mM AM (PMY, 0.6±0.14, n=4 vs PMY + AM, 0.16±0.03, n=5, t(3.2)=3.1, p=0.048; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D

claim: When applying 100 µM dopamine, the PMY signal was significantly increased compared with slices without dopamine.
source: Strikingly, when applying 100 µM dopamine, the PMY signal was significantly increased compared with slices without dopamine (PMY, 0.54±0.03, n=9 vs PMY + DA, 0.80±0.019, n=16, p<0.001; Figure 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental measurements shown in Figure 1B and C

claim: The D1/D5 receptor agonist SKF38393 (10 µM) stimulates protein synthesis to a similar extent as dopamine.
source: We next examined the effect of the D1/D5 receptor agonist SKF38393 (10 µM) and found that it stimulates protein synthesis to a similar extent as dopamine, with no significant difference between those two conditions (PMY + DA, 0.80±0.019, n=16, vs PMY + SFK, 0.79±0.026, n=9, p>0.99), and significantly different to PMY alone (PMY, 0.54±0.03, n=9 vs PMY + SFK, 0.79±0.026, n=9, p<0.001; Figure 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental measurements shown in Figure 1B and C

claim: The dopamine-induced increase in protein synthesis was prevented by the application of D1/5 and D2 receptor antagonists.
source: Using 10 µM SCH23390, a selective antagonist at D1 (Ki = 0.2 nM) and D5 (Ki = 0.3 nM) receptor subtypes, and 50 µM sulpiride, a D2 antagonist (Ki = 8 nM), we found that the dopamine-induced increase in PMY signal was prevented (PMY + DA, 0.80±0.019, n=16, vs PMY + DA + SCH23390/sulpiride, 0.61±0.029, n=8, p<0.001; all p values reported above from post-hoc Tukey's HSD test, after confirming a statistically significant difference between at least two groups in one-way ANOVA; F(4, 46)=49.55, p<0.001; Figure 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental measurements shown in Figure 1B and C

claim: Dopamine application significantly increased the PMY signal in western blot analysis.
source: Dopamine application significantly increased the PMY signal (PMY, 97±21, n=5, vs PMY + DA = 201±25, n=5, p=0.006; p values reported from post-hoc Tukey's HSD test after one-way ANOVA; F(3, 16)=19.85, p<0.0001; Figure 1D and E).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of western blot measurements shown in Figure 1D and E

claim: The application of dopamine after the post-before-pre pairing protocol (Δt = -20ms) induces robust synaptic potentiation.
source: We confirmed that the application of dopamine after the post-before-pre pairing protocol (Δt = -20ms) induces robust synaptic potentiation (138% ± 16% vs 100%, t(8) = 2.5, p=0.039, n=9; Figure 1F and G)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiology measurements shown in Figure 1F and G

claim: The same pairing protocol without dopamine application leads to robust input-specific synaptic depression.
source: while the same pairing protocol without dopamine application leads to robust input-specific synaptic depression (t-LTD 64% ± 9% vs control 106% ± 8%, t(6) = 5.8, p=0.001; Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiology measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and F

claim: Dopamine application alone had no effect on synapses that did not undergo prior pairing.
source: Dopamine application alone had no effect on synapses that did not undergo prior pairing (102% ± 14% vs 100%, t(8) = 0.13, p=0.89, n=9; Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiology measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G

claim: When delivering the protein synthesis inhibitor AM to the postsynaptic cell through the recording pipette, DA-LTP was fully blocked, leaving synaptic depression instead.
source: When delivering the protein synthesis inhibitor AM to the postsynaptic cell through the recording pipette, DA-LTP was fully blocked, leaving synaptic depression instead (DA + AM, 56% ± 9% vs 100%, t(5) = 4.8, p=0.0047, n=6), which was significantly different from dopamine without AM (DA 138% ± 16% vs DA + AM 56% ± 9%, t(13) = 3.9, p=0.0016; Figure 1F and G).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiology measurements shown in Figure 1F and G

claim: Loading CHX into the postsynaptic cell through the recording pipette completely blocked DA-LTP, leaving synaptic depression instead.
source: We found that loading CHX into the postsynaptic cell through the recording pipette also completely blocked DA-LTP, leaving synaptic depression instead (DA + CHX, 55% ± 12% vs 100%, t(5) = 3.7, p=0.013, n=6; Figure 1F), which was significantly different from dopamine without CHX (DA 138% ± 16% vs DA + CHX 55% ± 12%, t(13) = 3.9, p=0.002; Figure 1F and G).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiology measurements shown in Figure 1F and G

claim: Postsynaptically applied AM or CHX had no effect on baseline synaptic transmission throughout the 60-min duration of the experiment in the control pathway.
source: We also confirmed that postsynaptically applied AM or CHX had no effect on baseline synaptic transmission throughout the 60-min duration of the experiment in the control pathway (no pairing +AM, 104±17% vs 100%, t(5) = 0.23, p=0.83, n=6; and no pairing +CHX, 98±6% vs 100%, t(5) = 0.32, p=0.76, n=6; Figure 1—figure supplement 1H and I).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiology measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H and I

claim: When using a t-LTP protocol (Δt = +10ms) while CHX was loaded into the postsynaptic cell, robust potentiation was still observed.
source: In contrast, when we used a t-LTP protocol (Δt = +10ms) while CHX was loaded into the postsynaptic cell, we still observed robust potentiation (t-LTP +CHX, 158% ± 19% vs 100%, t(5) = 3.11, p=0.026, n=6, Figure 1H)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiology measurements shown in Figure 1H

claim: DA-LTP, but not conventional t-LTP, requires postsynaptic protein synthesis.
source: These results demonstrate that DA-LTP, but not conventional t-LTP, requires postsynaptic protein synthesis, revealing two different signalling pathways for LTP, one of which requires dopamine and protein synthesis, while the other one does not.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects of protein synthesis inhibitors on DA-LTP versus t-LTP shown in experimental data

claim: Application of TTX inhibits spontaneous excitatory postsynaptic potentials (EPSPs) in CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: We confirmed using whole-cell patch clamp recordings that application of TTX inhibits spontaneous excitatory postsynaptic potentials (EPSPs) in CA1 pyramidal neurons in our preparations (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology recordings shown in Figure 2B

claim: TTX incubation alone did not significantly alter PMY labelling.
source: Using the PMY labelling assay, we found that TTX incubation alone did not significantly alter PMY labelling, suggesting that the baseline level of protein synthesis is not affected by blocking neuronal activity for 30 min (control, 0.55±0.033, n=8, vs TTX, 0.53±0.026, n=8, p=0.90; Figure 2A and C).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of PMY labeling measurements shown in Figure 2A and C

claim: TTX significantly diminished the dopamine-induced increase in protein synthesis.
source: However, TTX significantly diminished the dopamine-induced increase in protein synthesis (DA, 0.83±0.024, n=9, vs DA + TTX, 0.65±0.017, n=9, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of PMY labeling measurements

claim: The dopamine-induced increase in protein synthesis was not fully blocked by TTX.
source: Nevertheless, the dopamine-induced increase in protein synthesis was not fully blocked by TTX, as it remained significantly higher in the presence of dopamine and TTX compared with TTX alone (TTX + DA, 0.65±0.017, n=9, vs TTX 0.53±0.026, n=8, p=0.005; p values reported from post-hoc Tukey's HSD test after one-way ANOVA; F (3, 30)=30.57, p<0.001; Figure 2A and C).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of PMY labeling measurements shown in Figure 2A and C

claim: The application of 30 µM Rp-cAMPS had no significant effect on protein synthesis in control conditions.
source: We found that the application of 30 µM Rp-cAMPS had no significant effect on protein synthesis in control conditions (control, 1.2±0.10, n=10, vs Rp-cAMPS 1.7±0.4, n=8, p=0.25)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of PMY labeling measurements

claim: Rp-cAMPS completely blocked the dopamine-induced increase in PMY levels.
source: but completely blocked the dopamine-induced increase in PMY levels (DA, 2.2±0.2, n=10, vs DA +Rp-cAMPS, 1.3±0.1, n=9, p=0.029; p values reported from post-hoc Tukey's HSD test after one-way ANOVA; F (3, 33)=4.912, p=0.0062; Figure 2D and E).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of PMY labeling measurements shown in Figure 2D and E

claim: DA-LTP was completely absent in AC1/AC8 DKO mice, leaving synaptic depression instead.
source: We found that DA-LTP was completely absent in AC1/AC8 DKO mice, leaving synaptic depression instead (AC DKO 74% ± 10% vs 100%, t(6) = 2.6, p=0.04, n=7), which was significantly different to DA-LTP in WT mice (WT 125% ± 16%, n=6, vs AC DKO 74% ± 10%, n=7, t(11) = 4.2, p=0.0016; Figure 2F and H).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiology measurements in AC1/AC8 DKO mice shown in Figure 2F and H

claim: Dopamine application after the t-LTD priming protocol followed by subthreshold synaptic stimulation failed to convert depression into potentiation in the presence of PKI.
source: Dopamine application after the t-LTD priming protocol followed by subthreshold synaptic stimulation failed to convert depression into potentiation in the presence of PKI (DA + PKI 81% ± 3% vs 100%, t(5) = 6.1, p=0.0017, n=6), which was significantly different from the effect of dopamine application without PKI (DA + PKI 81% ± 3% vs DA 125% ± 16%, t(10) = 6.2, p=0.0001; Figure 2G and H).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiology measurements shown in Figure 2G and H

claim: Dopamine application induces a significant increase in the GluA1 receptor subunit compared with control conditions.
source: Using western blot analysis, we found that dopamine application induces a significant increase in the GluA1 receptor subunit compared with control conditions (control, 0.43±0.069 a.u., n=7, vs DA, 0.84±0.07, n=7, F (1.8, 10.8)=12.04, p=0.013; Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of western blot measurements shown in Figure 3A and B

claim: When protein synthesis was blocked with CHX, the GluA1 increase was prevented.
source: Importantly, when we blocked protein synthesis with CHX, the GluA1 increase was prevented (DA, 0.84±0.07, n=7, vs DA + CHX, 0.38±0.05, n=7, F (1.8, 10.8)=12.04, p=0.037; Figure 3A and B)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of western blot measurements shown in Figure 3A and B

claim: The dopamine-induced increase in GluA1 is protein-synthesis-dependent.
source: showing that the dopamine-induced increase in GluA1 is protein-synthesis-dependent.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that CHX blocks the dopamine-induced GluA1 increase

claim: No significant differences in GluA2 subunit levels were detected between dopamine-treated and control CA1.
source: In contrast, when we measured the levels of the GluA2 subunit under the same conditions, we could not detect significant differences between dopamine-treated and control CA1 (control, 0.8±0.2, n=6, vs DA, 0.7±0.14, n=6, F (1.4, 6.88)=0.86, p=0.46; Figure 3A and C)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of western blot measurements shown in Figure 3A and C

claim: No significant differences in GluA2 subunit levels were detected in the presence of CHX.
source: nor in the presence of CHX (DA 0.7±0.14, n=6, vs DA + CHX, 0.76±0.19, n=6, F (1.4, 6.88)=0.86, p=0.87; Figure 3A and C).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of western blot measurements shown in Figure 3A and C

claim: A t-LTP protocol (Δt = +10 ms) led to synaptic potentiation in GluA1 KO mice, albeit of somewhat reduced magnitude.
source: We found that a t-LTP protocol (Δt = +10 ms) led to synaptic potentiation, albeit of somewhat reduced magnitude (t-LTP GluA1 KO, 125% ± 9% vs 100%, t(5) = 2.6, p=0.046, n=6; Figure 3D and F)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiology measurements in GluA1 KO mice shown in Figure 3D and F

claim: A t-LTD protocol (Δt = –20 ms) induced synaptic depression in GluA1 KO mice.
source: while a t-LTD protocol (Δt = –20 ms) induced synaptic depression (t-LTD GluA1 KO, 66% ± 9% vs 100%, t(12) = 3.9, p=0.002, n=13; Figure 3D and F).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiology measurements in GluA1 KO mice shown in Figure 3D and F

claim: In the GluA1 KO mice, the application of dopamine failed to convert t-LTD into LTP.
source: Strikingly, however, in the GluA1 KO mice, the application of dopamine failed to convert t-LTD into LTP (DA-LTP GluA1 KO, 90% ± 7%, n=8; Figure 3E)
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology measurements in GluA1 KO mice shown in Figure 3E

claim: The resulting depression in GluA1 KO mice was not significantly different from t-LTD without dopamine.
source: and the resulting depression was not significantly different from t-LTD without dopamine (t-LTD vs DA-LTP, t(19) = 1.905, p=0.07; Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiology measurements shown in Figure 3F

claim: Newly synthesised GluA1 subunits are required for the expression of DA-LTP.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that newly synthesised GluA1 subunits are required for the expression of DA-LTP.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations that dopamine increases GluA1 in a protein-synthesis-dependent manner and that DA-LTP is absent in GluA1 KO mice

claim: Robust t-LTP was elicited in the presence of extracellular NASPM.
source: We found that robust t-LTP was elicited in the presence of extracellular NASPM (139% ± 11% vs 100%, t(5) = 3.6, p=0.015, n=6; Figure 4A and C).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiology measurements shown in Figure 4A and C

claim: When applying NASPM during a DA-LTP protocol, potentiation was completely prevented.
source: In contrast, when applying NASPM during a DA-LTP protocol, potentiation was completely prevented (75% ± 15% vs 100%, t(5) = 1.66, p=0.16, n=6; Figure 4B and C).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiology measurements shown in Figure 4B and C

claim: CP-AMPARs are required for DA-LTP.
source: This shows that CP-AMPARs are indeed required for DA-LTP.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that NASPM blocks DA-LTP but not t-LTP

claim: The application of NASPM during burst stimulation completely prevented synaptic potentiation.
source: We found that the application of NASPM during burst stimulation completely prevented synaptic potentiation (78% ± 11% vs 100%, t(6) = 2.01, p=0.091, n=7; Figure 4D and F).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiology measurements shown in Figure 4D and F

claim: When applying NASPM 7 min after burst stimulation, an initial potentiation was observed which gradually returned to baseline in the presence of NASPM.
source: When applying NASPM 7 min after burst stimulation, we observed an initial potentiation (118% ± 4% vs 100%, t(6) = 4.52, p=0.0063, n=6), which gradually returned to baseline in the presence of NASPM (91% ± 11% vs 100%, t(5) = 0.82, p=0.45, n=6; Figure 4E and F)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiology measurements shown in Figure 4E and F

claim: The expression of DA-LTP is mediated by CP-AMPARs.
source: suggesting that the expression of DA-LTP is mediated by CP-AMPARs.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that blocking CP-AMPARs after induction reverses DA-LTP

claim: Conventional t-LTP (Δt = +10 ms) was significantly different from DA-LTP in the presence of IEM1460 throughout the recording.
source: Conventional t-LTP (Δt = +10 ms) was compared with DA-LTP in the presence of IEM1460 throughout the recording, which were significantly different (t-LTP +IEM1460, 142%±21%, n=7, vs DA-LTP +IEM1460, 80%±8%, n=7, t(12) = 2.75, p=0.02; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B and D).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiology measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B and D

claim: When IEM1460 was applied immediately after the pairing protocol, it still prevented DA-LTP and left a synaptic depression instead.
source: When applied immediately after the pairing protocol, IEM1460 still prevented DA-LTP and left a synaptic depression instead (DA-LTP +IEM after, 68% ± 12% vs 100%, t(8) = 2.68, p=0.028, n=9; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiology measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D

claim: DA-LTP, but not conventional t-LTP, requires CP-AMPARs for the expression of synaptic potentiation.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that DA-LTP, but not conventional t-LTP, requires CP-AMPARs for the expression of synaptic potentiation.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects of CP-AMPAR blockers on DA-LTP versus t-LTP

claim: Dopamine enables a rapid onset protein-synthesis-dependent form of synaptic potentiation (DA-LTP).
source: We report four main findings: (1) Dopamine increases protein synthesis in an activity-dependent manner through the activation of PKA. (2) Dopamine enables a rapid onset protein-synthesis-dependent form of synaptic potentiation (DA-LTP).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that protein synthesis inhibitors block DA-LTP

claim: Dopamine increases the level of GluA1 but not GluA2 subunit of AMPA receptors.
source: (3) Dopamine increases the level of GluA1 but not GluA2 subunit of AMPA receptors.
evidence: Supported by western blot data showing selective increase in GluA1

claim: The expression of DA-LTP requires GluA1 AMPA receptor subunit and Ca2+-permeable (CP)-AMPARs, whereas t-LTP does not.
source: (4) The expression of DA-LTP requires GluA1 AMPA receptor subunit and Ca2+-permeable (CP)-AMPARs, whereas t-LTP does not, suggesting the existence of two distinct forms of LTP.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from GluA1 KO mice and CP-AMPAR blocker experiments

claim: Two distinct forms of LTP exist at hippocampal CA1 synapses.
source: suggesting the existence of two distinct forms of LTP.
evidence: Inferred from the differential requirements for protein synthesis, GluA1, and CP-AMPARs between DA-LTP and t-LTP

claim: Dopamine receptor agonist SKF-38393 enhances protein synthesis in hippocampal and cortical neuronal cell culture systems.
source: This is consistent with previous reports from hippocampal and cortical neuronal cell culture systems, which showed that dopamine receptor agonist SKF-38393 enhances protein synthesis (Smith et al., 2005; David et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: The dopamine-induced increase in protein synthesis is mediated by dopamine receptors via the AC-cAMP-PKA pathway.
source: We found that the dopamine-induced increase in protein synthesis is mediated by dopamine receptors via the AC-cAMP-PKA pathway (Mayr and Montminy, 2001; Sassone-Corsi, 1995)
evidence: Supported by experimental data using receptor antagonists and PKA inhibitors, and by citations to prior research

claim: The application of Sp-cAMPS, an activator of PKA, was sufficient to induce an increase in protein synthesis in hippocampal cell culture.
source: which is also consistent with previously reported hippocampal cell culture results which showed that the application of Sp-cAMPS, an activator of PKA, was sufficient to induce an increase in protein synthesis (Smith et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: D1 receptors, but not D2 receptors, increase protein synthesis via the mTOR-ERK pathway in cortical primary neuronal cultures.
source: It has been reported in cortical primary neuronal cultures that D1 receptors, but not D2 receptors, increase protein synthesis via the mTOR-ERK pathway, resulting in dephosphorylation of eEF2 (David et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Burst-induced potentiation in the presence of dopamine requires postsynaptic PKA and protein synthesis.
source: Consistent with our previous results that burst-induced potentiation in the presence of dopamine requires postsynaptic PKA and protein synthesis (Fuchsberger et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research by the authors

claim: Protein synthesis was required hours after LTP induction for the maintenance of synaptic strength in L-LTP.
source: and it was reported that protein synthesis was required hours after LTP induction for the maintenance of synaptic strength (Frey et al., 1988).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: For DA-LTP, protein synthesis was required ahead of or within the first few minutes of the induction protocol.
source: In contrast, for the form of dopamine-dependent LTP studied here, protein synthesis was required ahead of or within the first few minutes of the induction protocol.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental design where protein synthesis inhibitors were applied before or during the induction protocol

claim: It is specifically postsynaptic protein synthesis that is required for DA-LTP.
source: Moreover, while previous studies have used extracellular application of protein synthesis inhibitors, here we loaded the protein synthesis inhibitors into the postsynaptic neuron via the patch pipette, suggesting that it is specifically postsynaptic protein synthesis that is required for DA-LTP.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental approach of loading inhibitors into the postsynaptic cell

claim: Neuronal activity was required for dopamine to increase protein synthesis.
source: We found that neuronal activity was also required for dopamine to increase protein synthesis.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing TTX reduces dopamine-induced protein synthesis increase

claim: The Ca2+-dependent AC subtypes AC1/AC8 are involved in the induction of DA-LTP.
source: Moreover, we identified the Ca2+-dependent AC subtypes AC1/AC8 to be involved in the induction of DA-LTP.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from AC1/AC8 DKO mice showing absence of DA-LTP

claim: AC1/AC8 is a coincidence detector stimulated by Gs-coupled dopamine D1/D5 receptor activation together with Ca2+ influx.
source: This coincidence detector is stimulated by Gs-coupled dopamine D1/D5 receptor activation together with Ca2+ influx (Wayman et al., 1994; Ferguson and Storm, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research and established knowledge

claim: The AC1/AC8 subtypes and PKA are required for DA-LTP.
source: Our results show that the AC1/AC8 subtypes and PKA are required for DA-LTP.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from AC1/AC8 DKO mice and PKA inhibitor experiments

claim: Dopamine application during neuronal activity induces the synthesis of plasticity-related proteins that enable synaptic potentiation.
source: These results suggest that dopamine application during neuronal activity induces the synthesis of plasticity-related proteins that enable synaptic potentiation.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations that dopamine increases protein synthesis in an activity-dependent manner and that protein synthesis is required for DA-LTP

claim: Dopaminergic signalling increases the surface expression of AMPA receptor subunit GluA1 in hippocampal primary cultured neurons.
source: This is consistent with a previous study in hippocampal primary cultured neurons which reported that dopaminergic signalling increases the surface expression of AMPA receptor subunit GluA1 (Smith et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: GluA1 plays an important role in LTP.
source: The selective increase in the GluA1 over GluA2 subunit is interesting because of the important role ascribed to the GluA1 subunit in LTP (Huganir and Nicoll, 2013; Diering and Huganir, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Conventional t-LTP could still be induced in a GluA1 KO mouse model.
source: We report here that although conventional t-LTP could still be induced in a GluA1 KO mouse model, GluA1 was required for DA-LTP.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from GluA1 KO mice

claim: GluA1 was required for DA-LTP.
source: We report here that although conventional t-LTP could still be induced in a GluA1 KO mouse model, GluA1 was required for DA-LTP.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from GluA1 KO mice showing absence of DA-LTP

claim: GluA1 homomeric AMPA receptors, which are calcium-permeable, mediate the expression of DA-LTP.
source: Furthermore, the findings indicated another intriguing possibility, namely that GluA1 homomeric AMPA receptors, which are calcium-permeable, mediate the expression of DA-LTP.
evidence: Speculative inference based on the selective increase in GluA1 and the requirement for CP-AMPARs

claim: CP-AMPA receptors appear to play a role in some forms of LTP.
source: CP-AMPA receptors appear to play a role in some forms of LTP (Plant et al., 2006; Guire et al., 2008; Frey et al., 2009; Wakazono et al., 2024), while other studies found no involvement (Adesnik and Nicoll, 2007; Gray et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research showing conflicting results

claim: CP-AMPARs are required for DA-LTP, but not for conventional t-LTP.
source: We report here that they are required for DA-LTP, but not for conventional t-LTP.
evidence: Supported by experimental data using CP-AMPAR blockers

claim: Blocking CP-AMPARs after the pairing paradigm reversed DA-LTP.
source: Importantly, even blocking CP-AMPARs after the pairing paradigm reversed DA-LTP, which supports the possibility that they are required for expression of DA-LTP.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that delayed application of NASPM reverses DA-LTP

claim: Two forms of NMDA-receptor-dependent LTP, induced by spaced and compressed theta burst stimuli (TBS), can be distinguished at hippocampal CA1 synapses based on their dependence on PKA.
source: Interestingly, previous studies have reported two forms of NMDA-receptor-dependent LTP, induced by spaced and compressed theta burst stimuli (TBS), that can be distinguished at hippocampal CA1 synapses based on their dependence on PKA (Park et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: The PKA-dependent form of LTP triggered by spaced stimulation leads to a transient increase in single-channel conductance, probably mediated by the insertion of calcium-permeable (CP)-AMPA receptors.
source: Additionally, it was shown that the PKA-dependent form of LTP triggered by spaced stimulation leads to a transient increase in single-channel conductance, probably mediated by the insertion of calcium-permeable (CP)-AMPA receptors (Park et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: The signalling pathway identified in this study overlaps with the pathway for PKA-dependent LTP triggered by spaced stimulation.
source: The signalling pathway identified in our study overlaps with this pathway and, together, these findings suggest that two mechanistically distinct forms of LTP coexist at these synapses.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of the current findings with prior research

claim: Two mechanistically distinct forms of LTP coexist at hippocampal CA1 synapses.
source: The signalling pathway identified in our study overlaps with this pathway and, together, these findings suggest that two mechanistically distinct forms of LTP coexist at these synapses.
evidence: Inferred from the differential requirements and mechanisms of DA-LTP versus conventional LTP

claim: Plasticity protocols that use extracellular electrodes may also trigger the release of dopamine.
source: It is possible that plasticity protocols that use extracellular electrodes also trigger the release of dopamine
evidence: Speculative statement about possible mechanisms

claim: LTP induced by spaced TBS may require dopamine receptor activation and protein synthesis.
source: and it would be of interest to investigate whether LTP induced by spaced TBS requires dopamine receptor activation and protein synthesis.
evidence: Speculative suggestion for future research

claim: The reward-related neuromodulator dopamine may contribute to protein-synthesis-dependent synaptic plasticity facilitating hippocampal long-term memory.
source: In summary, our findings suggest a possible mechanism for how the reward-related neuromodulator dopamine may contribute to protein-synthesis-dependent synaptic plasticity facilitating hippocampal long-term memory.
evidence: Inferred from the combined findings of the study

claim: Dysregulation in dopamine systems has been implicated in drug addiction.
source: Dysregulation in dopamine systems has long been implicated in drug addiction (for review, see Dalley and Everitt, 2009)
evidence: Supported by citation to review article

claim: Dysregulation in dopamine systems has been implicated in schizophrenia.
source: schizophrenia (for review, see Kahn et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to review article

claim: Dysregulation in dopamine systems has been implicated in Parkinson's disease.
source: and neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson's disease (for review, see Poewe et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to review article

claim: Dysregulation in dopamine systems has been implicated in Alzheimer's disease.
source: and, more recently, also Alzheimer's disease (Nobili et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Understanding signalling pathways underlying dopamine-dependent synaptic plasticity may help guide future research into additional treatment options.
source: Understanding signalling pathways underlying dopamine-dependent synaptic plasticity may help guide future research into additional treatment options.
evidence: Speculative statement about potential implications

claim: Timing-dependent synaptic depression (t-LTD) can be converted into potentiation by dopamine application during synaptic stimulation.
source: We have previously reported that timing-dependent synaptic depression (t-LTD) can be converted into potentiation by dopamine application during synaptic stimulation (Brzosko et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research by the authors

claim: Timing-dependent synaptic depression (t-LTD) can be converted into potentiation by dopamine application during postsynaptic burst activation.
source: or postsynaptic burst activation (Fuchsberger et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research by the authors

claim: DA-LTP is mediated via the Ca2+-sensitive adenylate cyclase (AC) subtypes 1/8, cAMP, and cAMP-dependent protein kinase (PKA).
source: Here, we show that dopamine increases protein synthesis in mouse hippocampal CA1 neurons, enabling dopamine-dependent long-term potentiation (DA-LTP), which is mediated via the Ca2+-sensitive adenylate cyclase (AC) subtypes 1/8, cAMP, and cAMP-dependent protein kinase (PKA).
evidence: Supported by experimental data using AC1/AC8 DKO mice and PKA inhibitors

claim: Neuronal activity is required for the dopamine-induced increase in protein synthesis.
source: We found that neuronal activity is required for the dopamine-induced increase in protein synthesis.
evidence: Supported by experimental data using TTX to block neuronal activity

claim: Dopamine induced a protein-synthesis-dependent increase in the AMPA receptor subunit GluA1, but not GluA2.
source: Furthermore, dopamine induced a protein-synthesis-dependent increase in the AMPA receptor subunit GluA1, but not GluA2.
evidence: Supported by western blot data showing selective increase in GluA1 that is blocked by CHX

claim: DA-LTP is absent in GluA1 knock-out mice.
source: We found that DA-LTP is absent in GluA1 knock-out mice
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data from GluA1 KO mice

claim: DA-LTP requires calcium-permeable AMPA receptors.
source: and that it requires calcium-permeable AMPA receptors.
evidence: Supported by experimental data using CP-AMPAR blockers

claim: Dopamine together with neuronal activity controls synthesis of plasticity-related proteins, including GluA1, which enable DA-LTP via a signalling pathway distinct from that of conventional LTP.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that dopamine together with neuronal activity controls synthesis of plasticity-related proteins, including GluA1, which enable DA-LTP via a signalling pathway distinct from that of conventional LTP.
evidence: Inferred from the combined findings showing activity-dependent protein synthesis, GluA1 increase, and differential requirements between DA-LTP and t-LTP

claim: Most hippocampal AMPA receptors are heteromeric, incorporating the edited form of the GluA2 subunit, rendering the receptor calcium-impermeable.
source: Although most hippocampal AMPA receptors are heteromeric, incorporating the edited form of the GluA2 subunit, rendering the receptor calcium-impermeable
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about AMPA receptor composition

claim: GluA1 may form homomeric calcium-permeable AMPA receptors (CP-AMPARs).
source: GluA1 may form homomeric calcium-permeable AMPA receptors (CP-AMPARs; Burnashev et al., 1992; Wenthold et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: By lacking GluA2, the extracellular N-terminal domain of GluA1 in GluA1 homomers is highly flexible, which alters the gating of the receptor and hinders its synaptic anchoring.
source: As well as enabling calcium-permeability of the AMPAR, by lacking GluA2, the extracellular N-terminal domain of GluA1 in GluA1 homomers is highly flexible, which alters the gating of the receptor and hinders its synaptic anchoring (Zhang et al., 2023; Stockwell et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: CP-AMPARs have been implicated in some forms of LTP.
source: CP-AMPARs have been implicated in some forms of LTP (Plant et al., 2006; Guire et al., 2008; Purkey and Dell'Acqua, 2020), including a PKA-dependent form of plasticity (Park et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Levels of the GluA1 receptor subunit, but not GluA2, were upregulated in response to dopamine in a protein-synthesis-dependent manner.
source: We found that levels of the GluA1 receptor subunit, but not GluA2, were upregulated in response to dopamine in a protein-synthesis-dependent manner.
evidence: Supported by western blot data showing selective increase in GluA1 that is blocked by CHX

claim: Conventional t-LTP remained intact in GluA1 genetic knock-out (KO) mouse model.
source: Moreover, DA-LTP was absent in a GluA1 genetic knock-out (KO) mouse model, while conventional t-LTP remained intact.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data from GluA1 KO mice

claim: Newly synthesised GluA1 receptor subunits mediate the expression of DA-LTP, possibly by forming GluA1 homomeric CP-AMPARs.
source: These findings suggest that newly synthesised GluA1 receptor subunits mediate the expression of DA-LTP, possibly by forming GluA1 homomeric CP-AMPARs.
evidence: Inferred from the selective increase in GluA1, requirement for GluA1 and CP-AMPARs for DA-LTP

claim: Blocking CP-AMPARs did not interfere with conventional t-LTP.
source: Indeed, while blocking CP-AMPARs did not interfere with conventional t-LTP, they were required for DA-LTP.
evidence: Supported by experimental data using CP-AMPAR blockers

claim: GluA1 homomers may form CP-AMPARs in the hippocampus.
source: GluA1 homomers may form CP-AMPARs in the hippocampus (Wenthold et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: A transient increase in CP-AMPARs has been reported in some forms of LTP.
source: A transient increase in CP-AMPARs has been reported in some forms of LTP (Plant et al., 2006; Guire et al., 2008; Park et al., 2019; Purkey and Dell'Acqua, 2020), including a PKA-dependent form of plasticity (Park et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research
